canonicalExplanation.summary: `git clone <url>` makes a **complete, independent copy** of a repository on your machine. It downloads every commit reachable from the remote's branches, records the source under the name **origin**, creates **remote-tracking refs** like `origin/main` (a read-only bookmark of where main was on the server when you last talked to it), and checks out a local **main** that tracks it. After that, your copy is **yours**: edits and commits stay local until you push, and changes on the server don't appear until you fetch.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner clones a class repository and edits README.md, then panics that they've just changed the teacher's project for everyone. They haven't. Cloning a public repository creates local origin configuration and an origin/main tracking reference while local changes remain entirely local. In this lesson you'll clone a sandbox repository and explain each local and remote-tracking ref.

```predict
{"question": "After cloning, you commit a change locally. Does the remote repository change?", "options": ["Yes, clone keeps them in sync", "No: nothing leaves your machine until you push"], "answer": 1, "why": "A clone is a separate repository that knows where it came from."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Branches, merges and conflicts** and **Branches as movable refs** (branches are names for commits).

sections.heading: The model: local branches, remote-tracking refs, origin
sections.body:
```bash
git clone https://github.com/example/practice.git
cd practice
git remote -v                  # origin  https://github.com/example/practice.git (fetch/push).
git branch -vv                 # * main 1a2b3c4 [origin/main] Initial commit.
git branch -r                  # origin/HEAD -> origin/main, origin/main, origin/docs.
git log --oneline --decorate -1   # (HEAD -> main, origin/main, origin/HEAD).
```

| Name | What it is | Moves when |
|---|---|---|
| `main`. | your local branch. | you commit, merge or pull. |
| `origin/main`. | your record of the server's main. | you fetch (or pull). |
| `origin`. | a saved URL nickname. | you change it with git remote. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Where is origin/docs checked out?", "answer": "Nowhere yet. It's only a remote-tracking ref. `git switch docs` creates a local docs branch that tracks origin/docs."}
```

examples.title: Cloning the practice repo
examples.situation: Cloning a public repository creates local origin configuration and an origin/main tracking reference while local changes remain entirely local.
walkthrough: **Creates local origin configuration:** git remote -v shows origin pointing at the clone URL.
**An origin/main tracking reference:** git branch -vv shows local main tracking origin/main.
**Local changes remain entirely local:** editing README and committing moves only main; git status will say "ahead of origin/main by 1".
examples.result: The learner understands their edits are private until pushed, and relaxes.

examples.title: The missing branch
examples.situation: After cloning, a learner runs git branch and sees only main, but the website shows a docs branch too.
walkthrough: git branch lists local branches only.
git branch -r shows origin/docs as a remote-tracking ref.
git switch docs creates a local docs tracking origin/docs.
examples.result: The learner can work on docs, knowing the difference between local and remote-tracking refs.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Clone creates a live shared folder where local edits immediately alter the remote repository.
misconceptions.correction: Clone makes an independent repository. Local edits and commits change nothing remotely until pushed, and remote changes arrive only when you fetch.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, what did a local commit change on the server?

analogy.example: Cloning is like **photocopying a shared notebook and taking it home**. You can scribble in your copy freely. A sticky note says where the original lives (origin), and another records what the original's last page looked like when you copied it (origin/main).
limitations: Photocopies can't sync; Git can, with fetch and push.
The last-seen note gets stale until you check again.

Step 2, Inspect: local is main; remote-tracking is origin/main, origin/docs. Local branches and remote-tracking refs are listed separately. Step 3, Commit: main is 5d6e7f8; origin/main is 1a2b3c4; server is unchanged. Local changes remain entirely local until pushed.

nearTransfer.prompt: Clone any small public repository. Run git remote -v, git branch -vv and git branch -r, and write one sentence explaining each ref listed.
expectedEvidence: origin identified as a URL nickname.

farTransfer.prompt: Create a bare repository as a sandbox remote, clone it twice into two folders, commit in one clone, and show with git log --all --decorate that the other clone's origin/main doesn't change until it fetches.
scaffold: Push from clone A, fetch in clone B.

remediation.explanation: For every name in git branch -a, ask: **is it local (I move it) or remote-tracking (fetch moves it)?** And remember **nothing leaves until push**.

recap.summary: To clone and explain each ref, remember clone makes an independent repository with origin saved as the source URL, remote-tracking refs like origin/main recording the server's branches at last contact, and a checked-out local main tracking it, with all local changes staying local until pushed.
